DESCRIPTION OF SOIL CAPABILITY UNITS
Capability Unit IIIe-2 Dryland
This unit consists of deep, sloping and rolling, fine sandy loam to silty clay loam soils. They occur on terraces, fans, footslopes, gravelly high benches, and loess mantled uplands. These soils are well drained and moderate to moderately slow in permeability. The available water holding capacity is 7 to 11 inches. Runoff is medium and the water erosion hazard is moderate. Soil blowing is a hazard on the benches near the mountains.
The frost free season is 105 to 415 days. The annual precipitation is 14 to 18 inches.
The soils in this unit are easily tilled. The soils on the valley footslopes need diversion terraces to intercept runoff from the soils above. The main water courses should be left in sod permanently. Crops respond to nitrogen and phosphorous fertilizer. Deep rooted legumes and grasses need extra phosphorous on the Danvers and Judith soils.
These soils are used mainly for small grains, alfalfa, and grass hay, and pasture. Small grains are commonly grown in a cropfallow system but they can be grown annually without fallow. Crasses suitable for planting are crested wheatgrass, smooth bromegrass, Siberian wheatgrass and green needlegrass.
Capability Unit IIIe-3 Dryland
This unit consists of deep and moderately deep, nearly level to sloping, fine sandy loam to clay soils. They are well drained and slow to moderate in permeability. They occur on stream terraces, fans, footslopes, gravelly benches, and shale and sandstone highlands. The available water holding capacity is 5 to 13 inches. Runoff is slow to medium.
The frost free season is 105 to 125 days. The annual precipitation is 11 to 14 inches.
Soils in this unit have a slight to moderate water erosion hazard. The soils with sandy loam, silt loam or clay surfaces are susceptible to moderate soil blowing. The soils occurring on the valley footslopes need protection from runoff coming from overlying soils. Water courses need to be left sodded to prevent gullying.
The soils in this unit are suited to dryland small grains, hay and pasture. They are also suited to range. Alfalfa, crested wheatgrass, and pubescent wheatgrass are suitable species for hay and pasture. Green needlegrass is also suitable on the moderately fine and fine textured soils.
